title: Aspiring Accreditor Approves First Institution
summary:
Aspiring Accreditor Approves First Institution
sara.custer@in… Fri, 10/23/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
The Commission for Public Higher Education—an aspiring college accreditor—announced Thursday that it has voted to give Florida Polytechnic University its stamp of approval, marking the group’s first accrediting decision since it was established in 2025.

“We set out to build a new approach to accreditation specifically designed to meet the needs of public higher education,” Mark Becker, chair of the commission’s board, said in a news release about the vote. “This decision represents the realization of that vision and an important milestone in the Commission’s development.”

CPHE has not yet earned federal recognition. That means the institutions it approves won’t be able to depend on CPHE alone to qualify for federal student aid. But the group is working through the yearslong process to obtain that recognition.

The commission was announced by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis at a press conference where he railed against the existing “cartel” of accreditation agencies, calling them proponents of “woke bias” and DEI. The governor specifically targeted the Commission on Colleges and Universities, formerly known as the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges.

CPHE has since received letters of intent from at least 10 institutions, including Florida Polytechnic. All 10 are currently accredited by CCU and located in Southern states—Florida, Georgia, North Carolina and Texas—where conservative lawmakers have criticized accreditation.

Florida Polytechnic and other institutions seeking CPHE accreditation will maintain their current accreditation at least until CPHE gains federal recognition.

The university, located in Lakeland, Fla., specializes in science, technology, engineering and mathematics education. Its choice to be part of CPHE, according to the news release, reflects its commitment to “institutional innovation” and “preparing students for success in a rapidly evolving workforce.”

“Earning accreditation from CPHE as its first institution is a tremendous honor and a historic achievement for Florida Polytechnic University,” President Devin Stephenson said. “This milestone reflects the dedication of our faculty, staff, and leadership … and we look forward to continuing our commitment to innovation, accountability, and student success.”

title: Higher Ed Leaders Go On Offense With Student Success Project
summary:
Higher Ed Leaders Go On Offense With Student Success Project
Joshua.Bay Fri, 10/23/2026 - 03:00 AM

More than 50 colleges and universities have joined a national effort to strengthen student success and reshape public perceptions of higher education.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
As colleges and universities face growing scrutiny over the value of a degree, higher education leaders are pushing back against skepticism, arguing that student success has long been an institutional priority, even if those efforts aren’t always visible to the public.

Against that backdrop, five higher education associations announced Thursday the launch of the National Student Success Project, a nationwide initiative bringing together institutions around five commitments to help students succeed both during and after college.

The associations include the American Association of Community Colleges, the American Association of State Colleges and Universities, the American Council on Education, the Association of American Universities, and the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities, with support from the Strada Education Foundation.

More than 50 colleges and universities signed on as initial participants, with many institutional leaders attending Thursday’s launch event in Washington, D.C. The project seeks to address concerns from students and families about the value of a college degree through five core commitments:

Deliver a strong value for the investment students make in education.

Empower students with clear and affordable pathways to a degree or other significant credential.

Advance academic excellence with innovative programs and strong teaching.

Ignite career ambitions through real-world experiences and robust guidance.

Cultivate a community that supports all students and promotes civil dialogue and respect for others.

Work on the project began earlier this year and has been guided by an advisory board of 19 presidents and chancellors from a range of colleges and universities, including rural-serving institutions such as Bemidji State University in Minnesota; faith-based institutions such as Baylor University in Texas; large public research universities such as Michigan State University and the University of California, San Diego; and community colleges such as Bunker Hill Community College in Massachusetts and El Paso Community College in Texas.

A commitment to student success: Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education, opened Thursday’s event emphasizing that the project isn’t intended to establish a universal definition of student success, but rather identify and address the barriers that prevent students from achieving it.

“What we’ve fashioned is an action plan, not around defining student success—that’s up to all of our campuses—but defining the things that stand in the way,” Mitchell said. “Those five commitments represent doorways that we need to open for students so that they can prosper and they can achieve success.”

“The people who scream the loudest that there is no value in higher education all have a college degree, and their children are all enrolled in college,” Chuck Welch, president of the American Association of State Colleges and Universities, said in opening remarks. “They understand that that value exists, and what we understand is that student success equals American success.

“Let’s educate more people and let’s not have these [flimsy] definitions about what success is,” he added. “At the end of the day, it’s about reminding America of how we got to where we are today and how we’re going to get into the future.”

Putting commitments into practice: During a panel discussion moderated by Inside Higher Ed Editor in Chief Sara Custer, Mitchell joined Bonita Brown, chancellor of Winston-Salem State University in North Carolina, and Linda Livingstone, president of Baylor University, to discuss college affordability, academic supports and career readiness as central components of student success.

Asked why leaders are launching the initiative now, Mitchell emphasized the growing need for higher education to shift its focus from internal academic discussions to publicly demonstrating student outcomes and rebuilding trust.

“I don’t think America believes that we care about students,” Mitchell said, pointing to low graduation rates as contributing to perceptions that institutions are failing students. He said the project plans to highlight successful practices through media outreach and regional convenings.

For Brown and Livingstone, student success extends beyond academics to encompass the broader campus experience. Brown emphasized the importance of life skills and workforce readiness, noting that even nonacademic staff, including housekeeping and landscaping employees, can contribute to students’ development. Livingstone highlighted Baylor’s use of co-curricular activities, such as intramural and club sports, to strengthen student engagement and retention.

“Student success from every aspect, every point of the institution, especially with HBCUs, it’s what we do,” Brown said. “It’s telling that story, taking that energy and elevating it, so we too can get some of those headlines and tell the story about the value that we bring.”

The panelists also emphasized civil discourse as an important component of student success, with Mitchell arguing that universities must “de-bubble” students by exposing them to diverse viewpoints to prepare them for life after graduation. Livingstone added that faculty also need training to facilitate difficult conversations effectively in the classroom.

“It’s a very divisive world right now, and we hear over and over from employers and others that they want students that can live and work in a diverse community,” Livingstone said. “We believe it is really important that our students understand how to engage with, to be respectful of and to live in community with people who think and view the world differently than they have.”

title: 5 Things to Know About Work Colleges
summary:
5 Things to Know About Work Colleges
Josh Moody Fri, 10/23/2026 - 03:00 AM

Inside Higher Ed’s recent two-part series on work colleges revealed what a select group of institutions can teach the rest of the sector.

Byline(s)
Josh Moody
full_text:
At most colleges, students work to earn money while they pursue a degree.

But at the country’s nine recognized work colleges, labor is built into the fabric of the institution, part of their ethos and infrastructure. And for some students, those jobs mean the difference between earning a degree and not attending college at all.

In recent months, Inside Higher Ed has visited work colleges and spoken with administrators, faculty members, students and supporters on and off campus. The picture that emerged shows a unique set of institutions that are focused on labor as both part of the educational experience and a pathway to financial freedom. And they use a model that aims to keep costs down and provide students with opportunities to help them find their footing in future careers.

Inside Higher Ed found that many practices that other institutions are increasingly adopting—such as an emphasis on demonstrable work skills and experiences—have deep roots at work colleges. And while the model holds significant promise for helping students graduate with less debt, or none at all, the sector hasn’t grown, due to significant costs and complexities.

Here are five takeaways from our reporting on this small corner of the higher education sector.

1. A Mission to Uplift Students

Work colleges are heavily focused on serving low-income students who have minimal resources to pay for their education. Financial need isn’t just a consideration in admissions; at some institutions—like Berea College, which only admits low-income students—it’s a requirement.

Student stories on those campuses are both hopeful and heart-wrenching.

Karen, a Berea student and child of immigrants who grew up a few hours away from campus in a small town in rural Kentucky, chose nursing because of her family’s experience. (Inside Higher Ed is not using her full name due to sensitive immigration issues.) Her father, who is undocumented, was diagnosed with diabetes, but he struggled to receive care and was turned away by some hospitals due to his immigration status, lack of insurance and a language barrier, she said. She also watched as her mother struggled with pregnancy complications with her younger sister, which doctors dismissed. Those injustices, she said, inspired her to pursue a career in health care.

But finding a pathway to pursue higher education was complicated, and she almost gave up on pursuing a degree before she even started.

“I originally was not planning to go to college. I had no way of paying for college,” she said.

Karen ultimately discovered Berea, which allowed her to pursue a degree that would have otherwise been out of reach. Now she’s working on a nursing degree with dreams of becoming a doctor and opening her own clinic to help patients like her parents who go underserved.

2. A Long Road to Recognition

Work colleges have been around for a long time—the designation hasn’t. Berea went tuition-free in 1892, and the roots of its student labor program stretch back even further. College of the Ozarks and Alice Lloyd College have also emphasized student labor for more than 100 years.

Congress didn’t create the formal federal work-college designation until 1992, though work colleges began collaborating in the early 1970s on ways to improve their model.

But federal recognition has not led to a surge of work colleges. The number of federally designated work colleges has long hovered at about 10. Some institutions with that designation have closed, such as Sterling College in Vermont, which shut down this spring. Others, like Bethany Global University, are no longer recognized as federal work colleges. But the sector has also seen new entrants in recent years, like Paul Quinn in 2017, Kuyper College in 2021 and Antioch College in 2024. Paul Smith’s College in New York is also making a push to become a work college.

The designation opens up access to some federal funding, including a small pot of money. Last fiscal year, recognized work colleges received just over $11 million in a dedicated federal appropriation—money that is split among those institutions. The designation also opens up more federal work-study funds, though colleges must make matching financial commitments.

They also must reapply for the federal designation every year.

3. Models Vary

While work colleges often share a similar philosophy, they differ in what jobs they prioritize and how the students’ jobs are structured, among other differences.

Three colleges have long-standing tuition-free models: Berea College, College of the Ozarks, and Alice Lloyd College (though the latter limits that offer to full-time students from 108 counties in central Appalachia). Berea recently announced that it would cover costs beyond tuition, while College of the Ozarks offers students free room and board if they work on campus over the summer.

Endowments help Berea and College of the Ozarks make those pledges to students—Berea’s is valued at $1.8 billion, while Ozarks’ is $703 million, according to recent figures. No other work colleges come close to those figures. A 2026 study found that some work colleges are still fairly reliant on tuition despite their models. For example, tuition made up 67 percent of revenue at Ecclesia College in Arkansas.

The work itself also varies by institution. Many work colleges place students in jobs on campus. Paul Quinn—the only historically Black work college—provides some campus jobs, but relies on corporate partners and nonprofits to provide student placements.

For far too long, folks have felt like what Appalachia needs is to throw money at it. What Appalachia needs is for folks to commit themselves to long-term solutions to long-term problems, and education can be the greatest equalizer if it’s given to folks in an equitable way.”

—Jessica Peña, director of admissions at Berea

But in the end, they all have to meet the same federal requirements, which include minimums for program participation, the number of hours students work in a semester and an infrastructure to help manage workers, track their hours and keep records of how they perform in their jobs.

4. Rooted in Place and Mission

Work colleges are spread across just eight states—Kentucky has two: Berea and Alice Lloyd. Of the nine recognized work colleges, most are located in rural areas, except for Kuyper College in Grand Rapids, Mich., and Paul Quinn, in Dallas. Those locations shape the mission and jobs available to students.

For instance, College of the Ozarks is located near a tourism hub in Branson, Mo., which opens up opportunities for students in the on-campus hotel, restaurant and event space. Berea has made significant investments in its craft program, in which students make traditional brooms and other items rooted in Appalachian culture. Multiple other campuses with large swaths of land lean into agriculture, forestry and conservation for student job placements, whereas Paul Quinn tapped into the booming business sector in Dallas.

For work colleges, their local communities often come first.

Berea recruiters, for example, don’t stray far from campus. Committed to serving Appalachia, the college has admissions staff in parts of Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia and West Virginia. Although Berea enrolls students from almost every state, it does not have national recruiters, but it does have partnerships with some schools in large metropolitan areas, such as Chicago. Berea also has a small international student population but doesn’t recruit abroad.

Jessica Peña, director of admissions at Berea, noted that many of the people leaving the region are doing so because of a perceived lack of opportunity. But Berea’s mission is to provide that.

“For far too long, folks have felt like what Appalachia needs is to throw money at it,” she said. “What Appalachia needs is for folks to commit themselves to long-term solutions to long-term problems, and education can be the greatest equalizer if it’s given to folks in an equitable way.”

5. Awareness Is Lacking

Multiple students said they had never heard of a work college before their search. Perhaps that’s unsurprising, since these nine institutions enroll only about 6,000 students altogether.

But students also told Inside Higher Ed that if they hadn’t found their way to a work college, they had no idea how they would fund their dreams. Some students said they wouldn’t have gone to college at all, due to difficult financial circumstances and a highly competitive scholarship environment.

Deina Reyes, a freshman from El Paso, Tex., was recruited to play soccer at Paul Quinn. Although Reyes said her grades were good coming out of high school, landing scholarships proved difficult, so she worked feverishly to help finance her higher education dreams.

“I started working as soon as I knew I was going to go to college, so I had two jobs at the time, trying to see if I could rack up some money before coming here,” Reyes said. “But I was really concerned. I couldn’t tell you how stressed I was. I signed up for every scholarship you could possibly think of, and I still didn’t even get 25 percent of them back. It’s really competitive.”

Now Reyes is an intern in the president’s office, working in a role that helps fund her education.

Azaria Powell, a freshman from Grand Rapids, was also uncertain of how she would finance her education until she found her way to Paul Quinn. Powell, who comes from a single-parent home, a low-income background and has experienced homelessness, planned to attend another HBCU until it proved far too expensive, even with financial aid.

“It’s just me, my mom and my sister, and we have faced adversity over the years. Back home, I am technically classified as homeless. I already knew when I started high school, and probably even early into middle school, that my mom was not going to be able to help me pay tuition,” Powell said.

She’s also an intern in the president’s office.

Paul Quinn President Michael Sorrell notes that high school counselors are stretched thin, and he believes that limited time with students means they don’t always offer a full menu of options.

“When you are hopelessly overworked, you look for the path of least resistance: state schools, publicly funded state flagships and regional institutions,” Sorrell said.

For Rock Azarro, it was a baseball coach, not a counselor, who introduced him to work colleges.

A junior at College of the Ozarks double majoring in accounting and finance, he grew up outside Kansas City, Mo., only a few hours away from the institution he would end up attending. But he didn’t know about the college until his baseball coach told him. Azarro was immediately drawn to the college because it was an answer to cost concerns, which loomed large for his family. He also liked the faith community and the idea of gaining work experience. Although he had never heard of work colleges, he now sees the experience as invaluable.

“It really sets up your future more than anyone could ever realize,” Azarro said.

title: Sure Pathways
summary:
Sure Pathways
Sara Brady Fri, 10/23/2026 - 03:00 AM

Solidifying the future is a bigger task than higher ed can do alone.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
When I headed off to college, back in the 1980s, my friends and I believed that there would be plenty of ways for college-educated people to make a stable living. Whether we went into engineering, law, medicine, teaching or business, we’d be OK. The main question was deciding what we wanted.

We didn’t have big money, but we felt like we had big futures. Even when things got hairy from time to time, as in the 1987 stock market crash, it literally never occurred to any of us that our future pathways were in danger. The occasional market crash or recession might have been annoying—honestly, I didn’t have enough money even to notice what the market was doing—but at worst, it was the equivalent of a thunderstorm. It might be messy, but it would pass soon enough, and once it passed, it would be as if it never happened. Graduating into a recession was frustrating, but the Bowen report assured us that there would be a tremendous hiring boom in higher education if we just hung in there.

Some of our hopes were false, but we didn’t know that yet.

I don’t see that same sense of certainty in students now. That’s not a criticism of them; they’re perceiving a changed world (mostly) accurately. Outside of health care, it’s hard to assert that a given path is a safe bet.

Remember when “learn to code!” was the answer to everything? AI ended that, and abruptly.

If you had asked me at, say, 19, if I thought I’d ever own a house, I wouldn’t have understood the question. Of course I’d own a house! Maybe not for a while, but it would happen. And given professionals’ salaries and house prices at the time, that answer would have been reasonable. (I say “would have been” because it literally never came up. That’s revealing in itself.) At this point, I routinely hear students complain that they’ll never own houses, and at current prices, some of them are probably right.

When people complain about the economy, it’s only partially about gas prices. Mostly it’s about the big-ticket purchases that determine a standard of living. Gadgets are cheaper and better than they’ve ever been, but places to live are much more expensive. There may be jobs available, but jobs that look like stable careers are much less common. How do you commit to a place and a person when a job won’t commit to you?

Tim Burke’s interpretation of Natasha Sarin’s recent column is well worth the read, but the issues are older than that. Jennifer Silva’s excellent books Coming Up Short and We’re Still Here, the first of which came out a decade ago, captured the core of the problem. The old markers of middle-class adulthood have become so expensive as to seem effectively out of reach for many, so they’ve developed other markers, such as overcoming trauma. That’s something, but it’s a lot grimmer than trying to decide between law and teaching.

On an individual level, there’s evidence that being well educated improves the chances of making a decent living. Evidence that a given major will lead to a job in that field is somewhat murkier outside of licensed professions. And I believe that whatever happens, skills like careful reading, discernment and some version of historical awareness are better to have than not.

Ultimately, though, solidifying the future is a bigger task than higher ed can do alone. Those professional pathways my friends and I envisioned and largely wound up living existed in a larger political economy that our colleges didn’t create. The fact that students now have a harder time making out a career pathway than my generation did isn’t a sign of a character flaw; it’s the result of seeing what’s there now. Yes, by all means, let’s prepare students as we can. But the real issue is much bigger than anything one industry does.

title: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
summary: The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests to form the biggest challenge to Vučić's rule.
full_text:
If Sunday's parliamentary elections really are a battle for the heart of Serbia, then who better than a cardiologist to be one of the leading figures in the race.

Ilija Srdanović appears an unlikely opponent for Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić, arriving for an interview by motorbike sporting a fluorescent yellow jacket emblazoned with pro-student slogans.

He has been selected as top candidate for an opposition movement posing the most serious challenge to Vučić since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) entered government in 2012.

The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests led by young Serbians, outraged by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station's canopy collapsed in Serbia's second city Novi Sad.

The Student List is up against a Serbian leader who has served successively as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since 2012. When he called these snap elections last month, he stood down as president to run again for the role of prime minister.

Whatever Vučić's title, there has never been any doubt that he was the man in charge – an image enthusiastically promoted by Serbia's largely uncritical media.

He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.

Vučić has painted the student movement as foreign-backed and seeking to "bring down our state". "Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at a final campaign rally.

Just like the protest movement from which it developed, the Student List has no hierarchy or nominated leader. This makes it a proposition unlike any other in Serbia's relatively short democratic history.

Reliable polls are thin on the ground, but analysts are predicting an extremely tight vote.

Ilija Srdanović may head the list of candidates – but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won.

Srdanović insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time."

The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes – and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness.

"We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name.

"All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds.

The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage.

At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources".

The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response.

Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands".

"This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED.

"Vučić has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy."

On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act.

Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China – both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.

Vučić has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power.

"When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally.

"You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart."

The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar Vučić as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates.

The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader – or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer.

title: Three signals shaping Australian international education ahead of AIEC 2026
summary:
From slowing student growth and tighter visa settings to the rise of transnational education, Australia's international education sector is entering a new phase. Ahead of AIEC 2026, The PIE looks at five shifts likely to shape conversations on the ground.

The post Three signals shaping Australian international education ahead of AIEC 2026 appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Australia is adjusting to a new era of managed growth

Australia’s international student market is showing signs of slowing as the sector adjusts to a more managed approach to international student numbers.

New preliminary government data shows overseas higher education commencements fell 4.9% year-on-year in the first part of 2026, from 130,415 to 123,968. Overall overseas higher education enrolments were broadly flat, declining 0.5%.

The slowdown comes amid another wave of policy change. New restrictions introduced in October 2026 mean most international students can now bring dependent family members only in limited circumstances, while the government has also tightened pathways for some temporary visa holders seeking to switch to a student visa onshore.

Those measures follow tougher financial and English-language requirements, the Genuine Student test and substantially higher visa application charges introduced in recent years.

At the same time, the government has maintained its National Planning Level at 295,000 new overseas student commencements for 2027, with provider-level allocations continuing to play a role in determining visa-processing priorities.

For students, the repeated policy changes are also feeding into how Australia is assessed against competing destinations.

IDP’s Emerging Futures research, released in March, found that more than three-quarters of international students are now “shopping globally”, comparing several destinations before committing to one.

“International students are highly attuned to policy signals, and they don’t just track changes in Australia; they’re watching the UK, Canada, the US, and emerging destinations at the same time,” an IDP spokesperson told The PIE News.

“That means Australia is no longer competing on reputation alone. It’s being measured side by side against alternatives on cost, visa certainty, opportunities for internships and work placements, post-study work rights, and how welcome students expect to feel.”

For institutions, the new environment is also changing how they approach recruitment and growth. IDP said the sector was responding by working more closely with government and thinking carefully about how it attracts students, manages demand and maintains quality.

“Australia cannot afford a race to the bottom on price or standards,” the spokesperson said. “The focus must remain on attracting genuine students, making good matches and delivering strong student outcomes.”

TNE is becoming a bigger part of Australia’s international education strategy

As Australia places greater controls on onshore student growth, its universities are simultaneously expanding their presence overseas.

India has become one of the clearest examples. The University of Western Australia opened its first Indian campus in Mumbai in September and began teaching at a second campus in Chennai in October, as Australian institutions rapidly expand their transnational education footprint in the country.

UWA is far from alone. Flinders University is preparing to establish a Bengaluru campus, while Deakin University and the University of Wollongong already have operations in GIFT City and several other Australian institutions are developing an on-the-ground presence in India.

The expansion suggests Australia’s international education model is becoming less dependent on students travelling to Australia, with offshore campuses, partnerships and hybrid models giving institutions alternative ways to reach students.

TNE could also offer a different proposition for students unable or unwilling to fund an entire degree overseas, while retaining opportunities for mobility between offshore campuses and Australia.

IDP said TNE has “real potential” to become a significant part of Australia’s international education offering, with its research suggesting students are increasingly considering it for reasons beyond affordability.

More than half of students considering TNE (52%) cited employment opportunities as a key motivation, while 49% pointed to reduced costs and 46% saw it as a pathway to future overseas study.

However, perceptions of quality remain a potential barrier, with 54% questioning whether TNE can match the main-campus experience.

“This reinforces the importance of institutions being transparent about their standards and outcomes,” the spokesperson said.

IDP also identified TNE as an issue it would like to see receive greater attention from the sector at AIEC.

“Australia has fallen behind international competitors in this space, and as debate continues around the number of international students on Australian shores, there’s a real opportunity for universities to grow by teaching more students in their home countries,” the spokesperson said.

Students are increasingly focused on values and outcomes

Australia is also competing for international students whose expectations of an overseas education are changing.

With the cost of international study rising and alternative destinations expanding their offers, employability, internships, post-study opportunities and return on investment are becoming increasingly important parts of students’ decision-making.

To remain competitive, Australia cannot afford to rest on its laurels as a lifestyle destination

IDP

As emerging destinations compete more aggressively for internationally mobile students, Australia’s ability to offer clear career outcomes, a strong student experience and confidence in the policy environment could become increasingly important to maintaining its position.

IDP said students increasingly judge value through career outcomes, course fit, skills and academic quality, rather than cost alone, with employability consistently outranking affordability as a measure of value.

“Studying abroad is one of the biggest financial decisions international students and their families will make, and they want confidence that it will deliver a strong return on their investment,” the spokesperson said.

“To remain competitive, Australia cannot afford to rest on its laurels as a lifestyle destination. It needs to combine high-quality learning experiences with clear pathways to employment, including internships, work-integrated learning and post-study work opportunities.”

title: Beyond the playing field: why sport matters in international higher education
summary:
Sport has long been recognised as a powerful diplomatic catalyst. For universities, its potential to build international relationships, strengthen institutional reputation and create a sense of belonging deserves greater attention.

The post Beyond the playing field: why sport matters in international higher education appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
When we think about how universities build their international reputation, we tend to focus on academic excellence, research partnerships, rankings and graduate outcomes. Yet another powerful way to connect institutions, countries and communities is through sport.

Sport transcends borders, cultures and languages. It creates shared experiences, forms relationships and generates goodwill in ways that traditional institutional engagement sometimes cannot. For universities seeking to strengthen their international presence, this represents an opportunity that extends well beyond the playing field.

At University College Dublin (UCD), sport is central to institutional identity. Our sporting tradition is reflected not only in competitive success, but in a sustained commitment to establishing opportunities for students to participate, excel and connect.

Significant investment backs that commitment. UCD is currently redeveloping its sports facilities, a project valued at more than €90 million. This includes new playing pitches, an athletics track, indoor tennis courts, as well as a large multipurpose sports hall.

Alongside investment in sports scholarships, coaching and high-performance athletic supports, these facilities reflect our belief that sport is integral to the university experience.

Sporting achievement generates considerable international visibility. At the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games, 34 UCD students and alumni represented Ireland on a global stage, including two-time Olympic gold medallist Paul O’Donovan.

Our Olympic athletes’ achievements bring recognition not only to themselves and Ireland, but also to the university community that has supported their development

Our Olympic athletes’ achievements bring recognition not only to themselves and Ireland, but also to the university community that has supported their development.

However, the diplomatic value of sports is not solely confined to elite competition.

Ireland offers a particularly interesting example through Gaelic games. Across North America, Asia, Australia, the Middle East, and elsewhere, international GAA clubs connect Irish diaspora with local populations, building networks around shared interests and cultural exchange.

For Irish universities like UCD, these networks offer opportunities to engage prospective students, alumni and international partners through an authentic expression of Irish identity.

Sport can also create new opportunities for institutional diplomacy. University engagement with international sporting organisations, national associations, overseas clubs and diplomatic missions can strengthen relationships that extend into education, research and broader international cooperation.

Indeed, UCD’s recent engagement with the Welsh Government Office in Ireland, which brought Olympic athlete Colin Jackson to campus, illustrates how sport can support bilateral relationships, connecting universities and governments.

There is also an important student recruitment dimension to sport. International students are choosing more than a qualification. They are choosing a community, an experience and a place where they hope to belong. Sporting opportunities, whether recreational or competitive, can help students integrate into campus life and develop connections that endure long after graduation.

For universities, there is a strategic opportunity to connect these different dimensions more deliberately: sporting excellence, student experience, alumni engagement, international recruitment and diplomacy.

In an increasingly competitive global higher education environment, reputation is shaped not only by what universities achieve academically, but by the relationships they build and the people they inspire.

Sport offers a compelling way to do both.

It is time we recognised it not simply as a key part of university life, but as an essential contributor to international engagement and institutional standing.

About the author: Una Watkins is director of international student recruitment and global centres at University College Dublin (UCD), Ireland’s global university. With over 20 years’ experience in international higher education, she provides strategic leadership for UCD’s international student recruitment, global market development and overseas operations, supporting the university’s international ambitions and global reputation.

Her work spans internationalisation strategy, global partnerships, market diversification and institutional positioning, with a particular focus on strengthening UCD’s international presence and engagement. A UCD alumna, Una has a strong interest in the role of higher education in international diplomacy, sustainability and the development of enduring global relationships.

title: Deeper Learning in College: 7 Student Engagement Strategies From Jal Mehta
summary:
Practical ideas from the Harvard educator on purpose, identity and getting students to do the real work of learning

The post Deeper Learning in College: 7 Student Engagement Strategies From Jal Mehta appeared first on Top Hat.
full_text:
It’s easy to tell when students are engaged in your lecture. You know the difference between a class where students are going through the motions and one where they’re invested. The harder question is what actually creates that difference.

Jal Mehta, professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and co-author of In Search of Deeper Learning, spent years visiting classrooms to find out what deeper learning looks like in practice. Mehta recently joined us on our Higher Listenings podcast to share ways instructors can create more engaging spaces in their classroom. Here are seven student engagement strategies you can try, no matter your discipline or class size.

1. Decide four ideas and four skills that must stick

Mehta is candid about how much of a course disappears from memory. “I know this is anathema, but we don’t remember a lot of what we learned in school,” he says. Even his Harvard colleagues, he notes, would fail parts of a test on material they haven’t used in years. His advice is to start with humility: “any semester is just a small taste in a lifelong journey to try to understand a subject.”

For a 13-week course, identify four big ideas and four big skills every student should have grappled with by the end. Once you’ve named them, it’s easier to let go of content that doesn’t serve them.

2. Treat every class as a pitch and open with a question

“Every time you come into a class, you’re essentially making a pitch,” Mehta says. He points to an English teacher who spends most of his planning time on the opening question, because if it doesn’t land, the rest of class is an uphill climb. Mehta agrees: “if that pitch doesn’t carry, then people are simply going through the motions.”

The best classroom engagement strategies start before anyone speaks. Open with a question or exploration, not an agenda slide. Then say why it’s worth wondering about and how it connects to the course’s larger arc.

3. Pause every 15 minutes for a turn-and-talk

Mehta points to research showing people struggle to take in information during prolonged periods. “After 15 or 20 minutes, unless you were a master storyteller, you will have people tuning out,” he says. When you see it happen, stop and pose a question. Have students turn to a neighbor and discuss for a few minutes. Then collect three or four comments from the room.

If that sounds familiar, it’s a close cousin of think-pair-share, one of the simplest active learning strategies there is. You don’t need to hear from everyone. The comments you do hear show you what’s resonating and what isn’t. A live poll or discussion question in Top Hat can do the same job in large lectures.

4. Make class more student-centered: let students do most of the talking

Mehta’s typical class structure is a model of student-centered learning: frame the day’s question briefly, give small groups of three or four an activity, debrief together, then add your own thoughts. Depending on the length of class, repeat the cycle. For more ideas like this, see our guide to active learning.

It also takes less prep than you might expect. “The person who’s doing the talking is doing most of the learning,” Mehta says.

Save your synthesis for after the exploration, either in a follow-up email or at the start of the next class. Written in advance, Mehta says, a wrap-up “feels too cooked.” Written afterward, connecting what students developed to what you know “usually makes it feel more alive.”

5. Teach the “whole game,” not just the parts

Mehta draws on his colleague David Perkins’s idea of the “whole game at the junior level.” His example: “you don’t spend a year throwing and a year catching and a year batting, and then say, when we get to graduate school, you’ll play baseball.” Kids play T-ball, and practice the parts in light of the whole.

He saw the same thing in a school theater production, where everyone knew what they were working toward and each student held a meaningful role. “One year you’re the learner and the next year you’re the teacher.” His diagnosis of most schooling: “schools have a lot of parts and not so many wholes.” Ask yourself where students in your course get to do a small version of the real work of your discipline, instead of just studying it from the sidelines.

6. Help students see themselves as people who do this work

Many students arrive with stories like “I’m not a math person” or “I’m a bad writer.” Mehta argues that “the most powerful thing you can do as a teacher is give someone a new identity:” start students on the path of seeing themselves as someone who does a kind of work.

After visiting summer camps, he came away convinced that “everything is a team sport,” and he’d like classrooms to feel the same way. He describes three levels:

Build a space where students can be themselves. Frame groups as a shared responsibility to help everyone move forward.

Look at who is in front of students. If every author on your syllabus looks the same, students will notice. The same goes for guest speakers.

Model your own curiosity. Come back from a conference and tell students what surprised you.

7. End class with an exit ticket

Not sure where to start? Mehta’s simplest suggestion is an exit ticket. Ask on one side, “what’s one thing you’re taking away from this?” and on the other, “what’s one thing that you don’t understand or are wondering about?” A TA (or a digital form) can sort the responses into piles, and the patterns will tell you what to address next class.

Deeper learning and rigor aren’t opposites

Mehta pushes back on the idea that engagement comes at the expense of rigor. Content versus skills, he says, is a false dichotomy. “You can’t offer an interpretation of the French Revolution without knowing who the Jacobins are, but what use is it to know who the major characters are if you’re not trying to do something with that knowledge?”

Some learning will always be tedious, he concedes. It just needs to be “in service of something that seems purposeful and meaningful.”

title: How one Fellowship spread beyond my classroom
summary: The post How one Fellowship spread beyond my classroom appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Lecturer Dr Chutrapee Popitikul, Nakhon Ratchasima Rajabhat University, Thailand, on how asking “what changed for others?” spread his Fellowship impact.

The short version

This year my teaching practice reached well beyond my own classroom: 111 colleagues from seven faculties; around 600 trainers in a UN-supported programme on green agriculture; 24 teachers in our partner schools, and my own students. The common thread is a question I took from the UK Professional Standards Framework (PSF) and Fellowship: what changed for others, and how do I know?

It started with “Referred”

My first Fellowship application came back “Referred”, meaning not yet successful but with a chance to resubmit. The feedback pushed me to stop describing my classroom and show what changed for students and colleagues, with evidence.

Rewriting the application changed how I work. I started looking for evidence of impact in everything I did, and I was already using that approach with colleagues before my Fellowship (FHEA) was confirmed in July 2026.

Working with colleagues

Nakhon Ratchasima Rajabhat University (NRRU) is a regional university in north-eastern Thailand. It runs its own recognition scheme, the NRRU Professional Standards Framework (NRRU PSF), which is aligned with the UK PSF.

In July 2026, the University appointed me as one of seven facilitators for a two-day NRRU PSF workshop for 111 academic staff from seven faculties. My sessions focused on how to build evidence that teaching and assessment work.

A UN-supported programme

Later that month, the Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE) in Thailand, with the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) as a lead agency, invited me to teach one module of a national train-the-trainer course on the Bio-Circular-Green (BCG) economy in agriculture. Around 600 trainers took part on site and online, including government extension officers, university-to-community facilitators and local project leaders. They will take the content on to farmers and communities.

My module covered monitoring and evaluating training. I used Kirkpatrick’s four-level model to move trainers beyond satisfaction surveys towards three further questions. Did people learn? Did they change what they do? Did it make a difference?

I applied the same thinking to my own sessions. Participants at my earlier workshops had asked for more practice time, so for this module I added more hands-on work and ready-made examples they could adapt. The rating for time and practice rose to 4.22 out of 5, up from 4.12–4.18 at earlier events. “I can apply this in my work” scored 4.38, the highest across my four training projects this year. These are satisfaction scores only, so I plan a three-month follow-up to see what trainers actually use.

Inside my programme

In the Computer Education programme, I facilitate one of three Professional Learning Community (PLC) groups set up in 2024. A PLC is a small group of teachers who meet regularly to work on teaching problems together.

When generative AI arrived in our classrooms, I drafted programme guidelines on the ethical use of technology and AI in teaching. The core rule is that students may use AI to support their thinking but not to replace it. The programme adopted the guidelines unanimously in May 2026 and asked me to share them with our partner school network. Twenty-four teachers there rated the guidelines 4.30 out of 5 for usefulness when setting work for their pupils.

What students noticed

For students, the changes show up every week:

• A short diagnostic test at the start of core modules, so I can match support to where students are.

• A fixed sequence in practical lessons. Students work through a knowledge sheet, then a practice worksheet, then a worksheet for recording their results. Rubric-based scoring comes last, with feedback and the option to resubmit.

• An early-warning system that uses Microsoft Teams and GitHub Classroom data to flag students at risk before they fall behind.

Students told us the sequence from knowledge sheet to rubric made the learning process valuable to them. Across four modules in the 2024 academic year (193 students), the average score rose from 54.9% on the pre-test to 78.7% on the post-test.

Where it goes next

In August 2026, I applied for NRRU PSF Level 3 and used the Fellowship process as my model. Senior Fellowship is my next step.

One thing to take away

Try asking one colleague this question: what changed for your students, and how do you know? That question is behind every change in this post.

How has your Fellowship changed things beyond your own classroom?

Dr Chutrapee Popitikul is a Lecturer in Computer Education, Faculty of Science and Technology, Nakhon Ratchasima Rajabhat University, Thailand, and a Fellow of the Higher Education Academy. He facilitates NRRU PSF workshops and a programme PLC, and has trained trainers for the UN-supported PAGE programme in Thailand.

title: Cybercrime: Anklage gegen Siebzehnjährigen wegen Missbrauchs von Minderjährigen im Netz
summary: Das Cybercrime-Zentrum Baden-Württemberg klagt einen Siebzehnjährigen wegen sexuellen Missbrauchs von Kindern und Jugendlichen im Internet an. Er soll zu einer Gruppe gehört haben, in der auch „White Tiger“ aktiv war.
full_text:
Cybercrime :

Anklage gegen Siebzehnjährigen wegen Missbrauchs von Minderjährigen im Netz

23.10.2026, 15:01Lesezeit: 2 Min.

Ludwigsburg: Seit einem Jahr sitzt der Jugendliche in Untersuchungshaft.dpa

Das Cybercrime-Zentrum Baden-Württemberg klagt einen Siebzehnjährigen wegen sexuellen Missbrauchs von Kindern und Jugendlichen im Internet an. Er soll zu einer Gruppe gehört haben, in der auch „White Tiger“ aktiv war.

Ein Siebzehnjähriger aus dem Kreis Ludwigsburg bei Stuttgart soll Jugendliche über Onlinespiele dazu genötigt haben, sich selbst zu verletzen. Rund ein Jahr nach seiner Festnahme hat das Cybercrime-Zentrum Baden-Württemberg (CCZ) nun Anklage gegen den Teenager bei der Jugendschutzkammer des Landgerichts Heilbronn erhoben – unter anderem wegen mutmaßlichen sexuellen Missbrauchs. Das teilten das CCZ und die Generalstaatsanwaltschaft Karlsruhe mit.

Dem Teenager wird vorgeworfen, einer Splittergruppe des kriminellen Onlinenetzwerkes „764“ angehört zu haben. Konkret lauten die Vorwürfe gegen den damals Sechzehnjährigen unter anderem: (schwerer) sexueller Missbrauch von Kindern und Jugendlichen in jeweils mehreren Fällen, die Herstellung kinder- und jugendpornographischer Inhalte, gefährliche Körperverletzung in mittelbarer Täterschaft sowie die Mitgliedschaft in einer ausländischen kriminellen Vereinigung.

F.A.Z.-Artikel häufiger in Ihren Suchergebnissen sehen

F.A.Z. bei Google bevorzugen

Bei der erwähnten Splittergruppe handelt es sich um die Gruppierung „Nefarious Maniac Cult“ (NMK). Der Teenager steht im Verdacht, jedenfalls im März und April 2025 Mitglied dieser Gruppierung gewesen und für diese als Rekrutierer neuer Mitglieder tätig gewesen zu sein, hieß es. Den Angaben zufolge besteht der Verdacht, dass die Mitglieder dieser Gruppierung das Ziel verfolgten, möglichst viele Opfer durch gezielte Manipulation psychisch zu kontrollieren und diese dazu zu bringen, sich selbst zu verletzen.

Er soll zur gleichen Gruppe wie „White Tiger“ gehört haben

Der damals Sechzehnjährige wurde den Angaben zufolge Anfang Oktober vergangenen Jahres festgenommen und sitzt seitdem in Untersuchungshaft.

Zum Netzwerk „764“ soll auch der im Juni in Hamburg festgenommene Mann gehört haben, der als „White Tiger“ bekannt wurde. Der Deutsch-Iraner soll Kopf einer Gruppe sein, die zahlreiche Kinder im Internet sexuell missbraucht und gequält haben soll. Unter anderem habe er über das Internet einen dreizehnjährigen US-Amerikaner in den Suizid getrieben. Die Staatsanwaltschaft Hamburg hat den Einundzwanzigjährigen unter anderem wegen Mordes angeklagt.

full_text:
«Un’alleanza tra pubblico-privato-terzo settore per i bisogni dei lavoratori, soprattutto giovani, e delle imprese». Dalla casa a stipendi adeguati al costo della vita, dal welfare alla formazione per l’uso dell’intelligenza artificiale. «Da detassare come si fa con i macchinari perché è un investimento per il futuro».

Chiedilo al Sole

sulla base del contenuto visualizzato.

La Compagnia delle Opere compie 40 anni. E alla vigilia dell’assemblea generale – sabato 24 alla Fiera Milano Congressi – il presidente, Andrea Dellabianca, anticipa con IlSole24ore le preoccupazioni – dal caro energia al risiko bancario alla Manovra alle nuove generazioni – e le priorità dell’ampia rete che rappresenta: 10mila imprese associate, soprattutto piccole e medie, per circa 60 miliardi di fatturato; 700 opere sociali e non profit sparse in 24 sedi territoriali e 9 internazionali. Istanze che prospetterà di persona al ministro dell’economia, Giancarlo Giorgetti, atteso alla convention. Al centro, la convinzione – eletta a manifesto - che “Nessuno costruisce da solo”. E che davanti ad un disagio dilagante, «dove lo Stato non riesce» occorra riconoscere al sociale la capacità di «far fronte a questi bisogni ed evitare degenerazioni».

Loading...

Partiamo da qui, la rabbia violenta di frange di giovanissimi e la protesta pacifica di migliaia di studenti. Le imprese avvertono una responsabilità sociale sul disagio dei ragazzi? Che pensa delle risposte dei decreti sicurezza?

Le regole devono esserci per controllare ed evitare degenerazioni, ma non risolvono la questione dei loro disagi. Occorre riconoscere e valorizzare esempi positivi di accoglienza ed integrazione che avvengono in molte scuole e opere sociali, capaci di una proposta educativa in grado di far intravedere una strada positiva ai giovani.

title: Intelligenza artificiale in Sanità: la vera sfida è la governance
summary:
Dalla sperimentazione all’adoption e alla sua integrazione sistemica nei processi di cura, l'AI apre a un nuovo percorso di trasformazione e innovazione in Sanità. Ecco lo scenario

L'articolo Intelligenza artificiale in Sanità: la vera sfida è la governance proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
L’AI apre una nuova fase della trasformazione digitale della sanità. Interoperabilità, data-quality, sicurezza, responsabilità diventano i fattori decisivi. Come spiega Andrea Leonardo, Healthcare Director di Almaviva, “il valore dell’innovazione non si misura dalla quantità di algoritmi introdotti, ma dalla capacità di calarli nei modelli organizzativi delle aziende sanitarie e convertirli in infrastruttura abilitante nell’assistenza sanitaria”.

Per anni ci siamo interrogati sulle potenzialità dell’Intelligenza Artificiale. Oggi la questione è cambiata. Modelli predittivi, AI generativa, sistemi di supporto alle decisioni cliniche e strumenti di analisi avanzata dei dati sono ormai una realtà consolidata. Eppure, alla rapidità dell’evoluzione tecnologica non sempre corrisponde un’analoga capacità degli enti di assorbire queste soluzioni nei propri processi.

Ed è proprio in questo gap tra innovazione disponibile ed innovazione effettivamente adottata che si pone una delle sfide decisive per il futuro del sistema sanitario: “Il problema non è più dimostrare che l’AI possa funzionare – osserva ancora Andrea Leonardo -. Dobbiamo superare la dimensione episodica della sperimentazione e costruire le fondamenta affinché queste tecnologie diventino – by design e by default – parte integrante dei processi clinici e organizzativi delle Aziende Sanitarie”.

La governance come condizione dell’innovazione

L’adozione dell’AI non può essere più affrontata esclusivamente in chiave tecnologica, ma richiede un modello di governance chiara e non negoziabile, ispirata a principi rigorosi di sicurezza e tracciabilità del dato, trasparenza, etica, nonché di ownership delle responsabilità.

La cornice regolatoria disciplinata dall’AI Act sancisce questa esigenza, soprattutto in un settore nel quale molte applicazioni incidono su processi ad alto impatto sulla vita delle persone.

“Quello della governance non può essere derubricato a tema di compliance normativa – sottolinea Leonardo -, ma deve essere disegnata ab origine nell’architettura delle soluzioni, accompagnandone l’intero ciclo di vita: dalla progettazione, allo sviluppo, fino al rilascio e al monitoraggio degli impatti”.

In questa prospettiva si inserisce la certificazione ISO/IEC 42001:2023 ottenuta da Almaviva, relativa ai sistemi di gestione dell’Intelligenza Artificiale: uno standard internazionale riconosciuto che certifica la capacità dell’organizzazione di adottare processi operativi a garanzia di una gestione virtuosa dell’AI e a tutela di bias o fenomeni distorsivi nel suo utilizzo.

Interoperabilità e dati: le fondamenta dell’AI

Nessun algoritmo, per quanto sofisticato, può dispiegare il proprio potenziale se il dato è frammentato, non interoperabile, non verificato alla fonte e, soprattutto, non validato dal professionista sanitario.

La sanità dispone di un patrimonio informativo straordinario, distribuito tuttavia tra ospedali, servizi territoriali, dispositivi medici e varie piattaforme digitali. La capacità di connettere ed orchestrare queste informazioni, preservandone qualità, affidabilità e semantica, costituisce il presupposto per rendere le applicazioni realmente efficaci.

“AI, interoperabilità, data-governance, cloud e cybersecurity non possono essere considerate dimensioni separate – analizza Leonardo -, sono anelli di una stessa filiera digitale, necessari nella costruzione di servizi digitali capaci di accompagnare l’intero patient-journey”.

È questa la logica distintiva alla base di HELIOS by GIOTTO, l’ecosistema della digital-health di Almaviva dedicato all’integrazione dei processi e alla continuità assistenziale ospedale-territorio. Con 17 progetti all’attivo, di cui sei regionali, 472 canali di integrazione e 28 sistemi integrati, HELIOS.connect rappresenta l’esempio concreto di un’infrastruttura abilitante per la trasformazione digitale.

A potenziare ulteriormente questa visione si affianca un altro asset proprietario: ULTRA, il framework lanciato di recente dal Gruppo Almaviva, che pone convintamente l’AI al centro dell’offerta, con una visione global declinata per mercati, domini, filiere produttive e settori mission critical come quello dell’Healthcare e la finalità di trasformare tecnologie e competenze in valore reale e misurabile per la Pubblica Amministrazione.

Intelligenza artificiale al fianco dei professionisti

L’introduzione dell’AI nei processi clinici pone inevitabilmente il tema del rapporto tra tecnologia e responsabilità professionale.

Il paradigma “human in the loop” assume un valore quanto mai centrale: gli algoritmi possono estrarre grandi dataset, individuare correlazioni e supportare le valutazioni, ma la decisione clinica deve rimanere fermamente nel perimetro del professionista sanitario.

“Il medico rimane centrale nell’iter decisionale, la tecnologia deve fungere da acceleratore delle sue capacità di analisi e di decisione -, chiarisce Leonardo -. Il digital deve liberare tempo, rendere le informazioni di facile accesso e consentire ai professionisti di concentrarsi su attività a maggiore valore clinico, salvaguardando quella dimensione relazionale che rende la cura del paziente davvero umana”.

In questa direzione si colloca, ad esempio, l’esperienza maturata da Almaviva con alcune ASL campane, dove l’AI si presta al servizio del professionista sanitario, estraendo grandi quantità di informazioni da cartelle cliniche complesse, referti, anamnesi ed esami diagnostici e sintetizzando elementi chiave che mettono il clinico nelle condizioni di maneggiare il giusto set informativo proprio nel momento in cui la decisione va presa.

Dalla pratica clinica al governo del sistema

Le opportunità dell’AI non si esauriscono nell’assistenza al paziente. Una delle prospettive più significative riguarda infatti il supporto alla programmazione sanitaria, all’anticipazione dei bisogni ed alla pianificazione delle risorse disponibili.

In un sistema chiamato a misurarsi con l’aging della popolazione, l’aumento delle cronicità e la carenza di personale sanitario, l’analisi predittiva può diventare uno strumento di scenario previsionale determinante nell’orientare scelte strategico-organizzative.

Con alcune Regioni, Almaviva sta lavorando ad ambiziosi programmi di applicazione capillare dell’AI, attraverso il rilascio di alcune POC su appropriatezza prescrittiva, liste di attesa e percorso chirurgico, con l’obiettivo di governare in modo dinamico l’equilibrio tra la domanda di prestazioni e la capacità produttiva delle singole strutture ospedaliere.

“È una delle dimensioni a più alto potenziale dell’Intelligenza Artificiale -, evidenzia Leonardo -. Non soltanto efficientare il flusso erogativo di una prestazione sanitaria, ma offrire al management strumenti per comprendere la distribuzione e l’evoluzione della domanda di salute, stratificare i bisogni e programmare l’offerta in modo più calibrato”.

Accanto a queste esperienze si sviluppano poi anche applicazioni verticali come HELIOS.Rehab che, integrando AI, biosensori e computer vision, supporta percorsi di teleriabilitazione anche a domicilio o il Progetto OncologIA, che ha visto l’utilizzo di modelli data-driven nel percorso oncologico e nella medicina di precisione.

Ecosistemi aperti e sovranità digitale

La progressiva diffusione dell’AI rende infine centrale due temi entrambi strategici: da un lato quello della sovranità digitale, che si traduce nella capacità di governo e messa in sicurezza del dato, evitando forme di dipendenza proprio nel momento in cui l’AI diventa così pervasiva e, dall’altro, quello del multi-vendor.

“La traiettoria dell’AI non sarà e non dovrà essere incentrata attorno ad un unico modello predittivo o algoritmo – , fa notare Leonardo -. Avremo bisogno di piattaforme generaliste e più verticali, ma in ogni caso aperte ed inclusive, capaci di orchestrare soluzioni diverse, garantendo sempre interoperabilità, sicurezza e sovranità nelle scelte tecnologiche. Per noi di Almaviva che siamo una Global Tech-Company con tecnologie, competenze, ricerca ed asset industriali radicati in Italia, questo rappresenta un pilastro strategico fortemente identitario”.

La prossima fase dell’AI in sanità sarà dunque meno legata alla proliferazione di sperimentazioni occasionali e sempre più orientata alla capacità di produrre risultati misurabili, sostenibili e replicabili su larga scala.

“In questo modo l’Intelligenza Artificiale potrà consacrarsi da fattore di sola innovazione a leva strategica per la tenuta a lungo termine del Sistema Sanitario», conclude Leonardo -. Ma questo accadrà soltanto se sapremo attingere da dati qualificati, integrarla nei processi operativi aziendali e governarne l’utilizzo con alto senso di responsabilità. Solo così potremo trasformare la tecnologia in creazione di valore per organizzazioni, professionisti e cittadini”.

L’AI apre una nuova fase della trasformazione digitale della sanità. Interoperabilità, data-quality, sicurezza, responsabilità diventano i fattori decisivi. Come spiega Andrea Leonardo, Healthcare Director di Almaviva, “il valore dell’innovazione non si misura dalla quantità di algoritmi introdotti, ma dalla capacità di calarli nei modelli organizzativi delle aziende sanitarie e convertirli in infrastruttura abilitante nell’assistenza sanitaria”.

Per anni ci siamo interrogati sulle potenzialità dell’Intelligenza Artificiale. Oggi la questione è cambiata. Modelli predittivi, AI generativa, sistemi di supporto alle decisioni cliniche e strumenti di analisi avanzata dei dati sono ormai una realtà consolidata. Eppure, alla rapidità dell’evoluzione tecnologica non sempre corrisponde un’analoga capacità degli enti di assorbire queste soluzioni nei propri processi.

Ed è proprio in questo gap tra innovazione disponibile ed innovazione effettivamente adottata che si pone una delle sfide decisive per il futuro del sistema sanitario: “Il problema non è più dimostrare che l’AI possa funzionare – osserva ancora Andrea Leonardo -. Dobbiamo superare la dimensione episodica della sperimentazione e costruire le fondamenta affinché queste tecnologie diventino – by design e by default – parte integrante dei processi clinici e organizzativi delle Aziende Sanitarie”.

La governance come condizione dell’innovazione

L’adozione dell’AI non può essere più affrontata esclusivamente in chiave tecnologica, ma richiede un modello di governance chiara e non negoziabile, ispirata a principi rigorosi di sicurezza e tracciabilità del dato, trasparenza, etica, nonché di ownership delle responsabilità.

La cornice regolatoria disciplinata dall’AI Act sancisce questa esigenza, soprattutto in un settore nel quale molte applicazioni incidono su processi ad alto impatto sulla vita delle persone.

“Quello della governance non può essere derubricato a tema di compliance normativa – sottolinea Leonardo -, ma deve essere disegnata ab origine nell’architettura delle soluzioni, accompagnandone l’intero ciclo di vita: dalla progettazione, allo sviluppo, fino al rilascio e al monitoraggio degli impatti”.

In questa prospettiva si inserisce la certificazione ISO/IEC 42001:2023 ottenuta da Almaviva, relativa ai sistemi di gestione dell’Intelligenza Artificiale: uno standard internazionale riconosciuto che certifica la capacità dell’organizzazione di adottare processi operativi a garanzia di una gestione virtuosa dell’AI e a tutela di bias o fenomeni distorsivi nel suo utilizzo.

Interoperabilità e dati: le fondamenta dell’AI

Nessun algoritmo, per quanto sofisticato, può dispiegare il proprio potenziale se il dato è frammentato, non interoperabile, non verificato alla fonte e, soprattutto, non validato dal professionista sanitario.

La sanità dispone di un patrimonio informativo straordinario, distribuito tuttavia tra ospedali, servizi territoriali, dispositivi medici e varie piattaforme digitali. La capacità di connettere ed orchestrare queste informazioni, preservandone qualità, affidabilità e semantica, costituisce il presupposto per rendere le applicazioni realmente efficaci.

“AI, interoperabilità, data-governance, cloud e cybersecurity non possono essere considerate dimensioni separate – analizza Leonardo -, sono anelli di una stessa filiera digitale, necessari nella costruzione di servizi digitali capaci di accompagnare l’intero patient-journey”.

È questa la logica distintiva alla base di HELIOS by GIOTTO, l’ecosistema della digital-health di Almaviva dedicato all’integrazione dei processi e alla continuità assistenziale ospedale-territorio. Con 17 progetti all’attivo, di cui sei regionali, 472 canali di integrazione e 28 sistemi integrati, HELIOS.connect rappresenta l’esempio concreto di un’infrastruttura abilitante per la trasformazione digitale.

A potenziare ulteriormente questa visione si affianca un altro asset proprietario: ULTRA, il framework lanciato di recente dal Gruppo Almaviva, che pone convintamente l’AI al centro dell’offerta, con una visione global declinata per mercati, domini, filiere produttive e settori mission critical come quello dell’Healthcare e la finalità di trasformare tecnologie e competenze in valore reale e misurabile per la Pubblica Amministrazione.

Intelligenza artificiale al fianco dei professionisti

L’introduzione dell’AI nei processi clinici pone inevitabilmente il tema del rapporto tra tecnologia e responsabilità professionale.

Il paradigma “human in the loop” assume un valore quanto mai centrale: gli algoritmi possono estrarre grandi dataset, individuare correlazioni e supportare le valutazioni, ma la decisione clinica deve rimanere fermamente nel perimetro del professionista sanitario.

“Il medico rimane centrale nell’iter decisionale, la tecnologia deve fungere da acceleratore delle sue capacità di analisi e di decisione -, chiarisce Leonardo -. Il digital deve liberare tempo, rendere le informazioni di facile accesso e consentire ai professionisti di concentrarsi su attività a maggiore valore clinico, salvaguardando quella dimensione relazionale che rende la cura del paziente davvero umana”.

In questa direzione si colloca, ad esempio, l’esperienza maturata da Almaviva con alcune ASL campane, dove l’AI si presta al servizio del professionista sanitario, estraendo grandi quantità di informazioni da cartelle cliniche complesse, referti, anamnesi ed esami diagnostici e sintetizzando elementi chiave che mettono il clinico nelle condizioni di maneggiare il giusto set informativo proprio nel momento in cui la decisione va presa.
